entries.575d591d1aa10c96bc7abedc573c1b064ead92f6: <div sID="gen7700" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="1Chr.8" sID="1Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen7700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7701" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7702" type="x-p"/> We had some account given us of Benjamin in the foregoing chapter; here we have a larger catalogue of the great men of that tribe. 1. Because of that tribe Saul came, the first king of Israel, to the story of whom the sacred writer is hastening, <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.1">ch. x. 1</reference>. 2. Because that tribe clave to Judah, inhabited much of Jerusalem, was one of the two tribes that went into captivity, and returned back; and that story also he has an eye to, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1">ch. ix. 1</reference>. Here is, I. Some of the heads of that tribe named, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.1-1Chr.8.32">ver. 1-32</reference>. II. A more particular account of the family of Saul, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.30-1Chr.8.40">ver. 33-40</reference>.
entries.17e4ac9f18306e390e845043672f9b7b08c0407a: <div eID="gen7702" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7701" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1660.)</title> <div sID="gen7703" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third, <hi type="super">2</hi> Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the sons of Bela were, Addar, and Gera, and Abihud, <hi type="super">4</hi> And Abishua, and Naaman, and Ahoah, <hi type="super">5</hi> And Gera, and Shephuphan, and Huram. <hi type="super">6</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Ehud: these are the heads of the fathers of the inhabitants of Geba, and they removed them to Manahath: <hi type="super">7</hi> And Naaman, and Ahiah, and Gera, he removed them, and begat Uzza, and Ahihud. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Shaharaim begat <hi type="italic">children</hi> in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara <hi type="italic">were</hi> his wives. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he begat of Hodesh his wife, Jobab, and Zibia, and Mesha, and Malcham, <hi type="super">10</hi> And Jeuz, and Shachia, and Mirma. These <hi type="italic">were</hi> his sons, heads of the fathers. <hi type="super">11</hi> And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal. <hi type="super">12</hi> The sons of Elpaal; Eber, and Misham, and Shamed, who built Ono, and Lod, with the towns thereof: <hi type="super">13</hi> Beriah also, and Shema, who <hi type="italic">were</hi> heads of the fathers of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who drove away the inhabitants of Gath: <hi type="super">14</hi> And Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth, <hi type="super">15</hi> And Zebadiah, and Arad, and Ader, <hi type="super">16</hi> And Michael, and Ispah, and Joha, the sons of Beriah; <hi type="super">17</hi> And Zebadiah, and Meshullam, and Hezeki, and Heber, <hi type="super">18</hi> Ishmerai also, and Jezliah, and Jobab, the sons of Elpaal; <hi type="super">19</hi> And Jakim, and Zichri, and Zabdi, <hi type="super">20</hi> And Elienai, and Zilthai, and Eliel, <hi type="super">21</hi> And Adaiah, and Beraiah, and Shimrath, the sons of Shimhi; <hi type="super">22</hi> And Ishpan, and Heber, and Eliel, <hi type="super">23</hi> And Abdon, and Zichri, and Hanan, <hi type="super">24</hi> And Hananiah, and Elam, and Antothijah, <hi type="super">25</hi> And Iphedeiah, and Penuel, the sons of Shashak; <hi type="super">26</hi> And Shamsherai, and Shehariah, and Athaliah, <hi type="super">27</hi> And Jaresiah, and Eliah, and Zichri, the sons of Jeroham. <hi type="super">28</hi> These <hi type="italic">were</hi> heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief <hi type="italic">men.</hi> These dwelt in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">29</hi> And at Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon; whose wife's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Maachah: <hi type="super">30</hi> And his firstborn son Abdon, and Zur, and Kish, and Baal, and Nadab, <hi type="super">31</hi> And Gedor, and Ahio, and Zacher. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Mikloth begat Shimeah. And these also dwelt with their brethren in Jerusalem, over against them. <div eID="gen7703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7704" type="x-p"/> There is little or nothing of history in all these verses; we have not therefore much to observe. 1. As to the difficulties that occur in this and the foregoing genealogies we need not perplex ourselves. I presume Ezra took them as he found them <hi type="italic">in the books of the kings of Israel and Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1">ch. ix. 1</reference>), according as they were given in by the several tribes, each observing what method they thought fit. Hence some <hi type="italic">as</hi>cend, others <hi type="italic">de</hi>secnd; some have <hi type="italic">numbers</hi> affixed, others <hi type="italic">places;</hi> some have historical remarks intermixed, others have not; some are shorter, others longer; some agree with other records, others differ; some, it is likely, were torn, erased, and blotted, others more legible. Those of Dan and Reuben were entirely lost. This holy man wrote as he was moved by the Holy Ghost; but there was no necessity for the making up of the defects, no, nor for the rectifying of the mistakes, of these genealogies by inspiration. It was sufficient that he copied them out as they came into his hand, or so much of them as was requisite to the present purpose, which was the directing of the returned captives to settle as nearly as they could with those of their own family, and in the places of their former residence. We may suppose that many things in these genealogies which to us seem intricate, abrupt, and perplexed, were plain and easy to them then (who knew how to fill up the deficiencies) and abundantly answered the intention of the publishing of them. 2. Many great and mighty nations there were now in being upon earth, and many illustrious men in them, whose names are buried in perpetual oblivion, while the names of multitudes of the Israel of God are here carefully preserved in everlasting remembrance. They are <hi type="italic">Jasher, Jeshurun—just ones,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the memory of the just is blessed.</hi> Many of these we have reason to fear, came short of everlasting honour (for even the wicked kings of Judah come into the genealogy), yet the perpetuating of their names here was a figure of the writing of the names of all God's spiritual Israel in the Lamb's book of life. 3. This tribe of Benjamin was once brought to a very low ebb, in the time of the judges, upon the occasion of the iniquity of Gibeah, when only 600 men escaped the sword of justice; and yet, in these genealogies, it makes as good a figure as almost any of the tribes: for it is the honour of God to help the weakest and raise up those that are most diminished and abased. 4. Here is mention of one Ehud (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.6">v. 6</reference>), in the preceding verse of one Gera (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.5">v. 5</reference>) and (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.8">v. 8</reference>) of one that descended from him, that <hi type="italic">begat children in the country of Moab,</hi> which inclines me to think it was that Ehud who was the second of the judges of Israel; for he is said to be <hi type="italic">the son of Gera</hi> and <hi type="italic">a Benjamite</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.15">Judg. iii. 15</reference>), and he delivered Israel from the oppression of the Moabites by killing the king of Moab, which might give him a greater sway in the country of Moab than we find evidence of in his history and might occasion some of his posterity to settle there. 5. Here is mention of some of the Benjamites that <hi type="italic">drove away the inhabitants of Gath</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13">v. 13</reference>), perhaps those that had slain the Ephraimites (<reference osisRef="1Chr.7.21">ch. vii. 21</reference>) or their posterity, by way of reprisal: and one of those that did this piece of justice was named <hi type="italic">Beriah</hi> too, that name in which the memorial of that injury was preserved. 6. Particular notice is taken of those that <hi type="italic">dwelt in Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.28">v. 28</reference> and again <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.32">v. 32</reference>), that those whose ancestors had had their residence there might thereby be induced, at their return from captivity, to settle there too, which, for aught that appears, few were willing to do, because it was the post of danger: and therefore we find (<reference osisRef="Neh.11.2">Neh. xi. 2</reference>) <hi type="italic">the people blessed those that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem,</hi> the greater part being inclined to prefer the cities of Judah. Those whose godly parents had their conversation in the new Jerusalem should thereby be engaged to set their faces thitherward and pursue the way thither, whatever it cost them.
entries.3399ae5ed72014a7daa616341eb35a78d58cfdc3: <div eID="gen7704" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 700.)</title> <div sID="gen7705" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> And Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul, and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Esh-baal. <hi type="super">34</hi> And the son of Jonathan <hi type="italic">was</hi> Merib-baal; and Merib-baal begat <reference osisRef="Mic.35">Micah.   35</reference> And the sons of Micah <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Pithon, and Melech, and Tarea, and Ahaz. <hi type="super">36</hi> And Ahaz begat Jehoadah; and Jehoadah begat Alemeth, and Azmaveth, and Zimri; and Zimri begat Moza, <hi type="super">37</hi> And Moza begat Binea: Rapha <hi type="italic">was</hi> his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son: <hi type="super">38</hi> And Azel had six sons, whose names <hi type="italic">are</hi> these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan. All these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the sons of Azel. <hi type="super">39</hi> And the sons of Eshek his brother <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Ulam his firstborn, Jehush the second, and Eliphelet the third. <hi type="super">40</hi> And the sons of Ulam were mighty men of valour, archers, and had many sons, and sons' sons, a hundred and fifty. All these <hi type="italic">are</hi> of the sons of Benjamin. <div eID="gen7705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7706" type="x-p"/> It is observable that among all the genealogies of the tribes there is no mention of any of the kings of Israel after the defection from the house of David, much less of their families; not a word of Jeroboam's house or Baasha's, of Umri's or Jehu's; for they were all idolaters. But of the family of Saul, which was the royal family before the elevation of David, we have here a particular account. 1. Before Saul, Kish and Ner only are named, his father and grandfather, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33">v. 33</reference>. His pedigree is carried higher <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1 Sam. ix. 1</reference>, only there Kish is said to be <hi type="italic">the son of Abiel,</hi> here <hi type="italic">of Ner.</hi> He was in truth the son of Ner but the grandson of Abiel, as appears by <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.51">1 Sam. xiv. 51</reference>, where it is said that <hi type="italic">Ner was the son of Abiel,</hi> and that Abner, who was the son of Ner, was Saul's uncle (that is, his father's brother); therefore his father was also the son of Ner. It is common in all languages to put sons for grandsons and other descendents, much more in the scanty language of the <reference osisRef="Heb.2">Hebrews. 2</reference>. After Saul, divers of his sons are named, but the posterity of none of them, save Jonathan only, who was blessed with numerous issue and those honoured with a place in the sacred genealogies for the sake of his sincere kindness to David. The line of Jonathan is drawn down here for about ten generations. Perhaps David was, in a particular manner, careful to preserve that, and assigned it a page by itself, because of the covenant made between his seed and Jonathan's seed forever, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.15">1 Sam. xx. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.23">23</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.42">42</reference>. This genealogy ends in Ulam, whose family became famous in the tribe of Benjamin for the number of its valiant men. Of that one man's posterity there were, as it should seem, at one time, 150 archers brought into the field of battle, that were <hi type="italic">mighty men of valour,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.40">v. 40</reference>. That is taken notice of concerning them which is more a man's praise than his pomp or wealth is, that they were qualified to serve their country.  <chapter eID="1Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen7706" type="x-p"/>

entries.31d636ca55425a16f95a574bd5e642182d17e25d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3703"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen5302" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.1-1Chr.8.32">1Ch 8:1-32</reference>. Sons and Chief Men of Benjamin.<div eID="gen5302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3703"/><hi type="bold">1. Now Benjamin begat, &c.--</hi>This chapter contains some supplementary particulars in addition to what has been already said regarding the tribe of Benjamin (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.6">1Ch 7:6</reference>). The names of many of the persons mentioned are different from those given by Moses--a diversity which may be accounted for in part on grounds formerly stated, namely, either that the persons had more than one name, or that the word "sons" is used in a loose sense for grandsons or descendants. But there are other circumstances to be taken into account in considering the details of this chapter; namely, first, that the genealogies of the Benjamites were disordered or destroyed by the almost total extermination of this tribe (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.11-Judg.20.48">Jud 20:11-48</reference>); secondly, that a great number of Benjamites, born in Assyria, are mentioned here, who returned from the long captivity in Babylon, and established themselves--some in Jerusalem, others in different parts of Judea. There were more returned from Babylon of the families belonging to this tribe than to any other except Judah; and hence many strange names are here introduced; some of which will be found in the list of the restored exiles (compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.1-Ezra.2.70">Ezr 2:1-70</reference>). <div eID="gen5303" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce7c110c96203200045a8d473eb8d512b52db431: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3704"/><div sID="gen5304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3704"/><hi type="bold">6. these are the sons of Ehud--</hi>most probably the judge of Israel (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.15">Jud 3:15</reference>). His descendants, who had at first been established in Geba in Benjamin, emigrated in a body under the direction of Gera (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.7">1Ch 8:7</reference>) to Manahath, where their increased numbers would find more ample accommodation. Manahath was within the territory of Judah. <div eID="gen5304" type="x-p"/>
entries.54038aca05f39aa71909fc24eecc0e7905024c4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3705"/><div sID="gen5305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3705"/><hi type="bold">8. Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab--</hi>He had probably been driven to take refuge in that foreign land on the same calamitous occasion that forced Elimelech to emigrate thither (<reference osisRef="Ruth.1.1">Ru 1:1</reference>). But, destitute of natural affection, he forsook or divorced his two wives, and in the land of his sojourn married a third, by whom he had several sons. But there is another explanation given of the conduct of this Benjamite polygamist. His children by Hushim are mentioned (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.11">1Ch 8:11</reference>), while his other wife is unnoticed. Hence it has been thought probable that it is Baara who is mentioned under the name of Hodesh, so called because her husband, after long desertion, returned and cohabited with her as before. <div eID="gen5305" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c7ab869c00b903af29a4028d882ed2ee4d095b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3706"/><div sID="gen5306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3706"/><hi type="bold">28. These dwelt in Jerusalem--</hi>The ordinary and stated inhabitants of Jerusalem were Judahites, Benjamites, and Levites. But at the time referred to here, the chiefs or heads of the principal families who are enumerated (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.14-1Chr.8.27">1Ch 8:14-27</reference>) established themselves in the city after their return from the captivity.<div eID="gen5306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5307" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33-1Chr.8.40">1Ch 8:33-40</reference>. Stock of Saul and Jonathan. <div eID="gen5307" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4babfa1b66170fabc5a0aed925b3444bf80d3ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3707"/><div sID="gen5308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3707"/><hi type="bold">33. Ner begat Kish--</hi>The father of Ner, though not mentioned here, is stated (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35">1Ch 9:35</reference>) to have been Jehiel. Moreover, the father of Kish is said (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference>) to have been Abiel, the son of Zeror, whence it would seem that Abiel and Ner were names of the same person.<div eID="gen5308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Abinadab--</hi>the same as Ishui (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49">1Sa 14:49</reference>).<div eID="gen5309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Esh-baal--</hi>that is, Ish-bosheth. <div eID="gen5310" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b6f4201e94edfe17d809b78c3f9c86dceff925b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3708"/><div sID="gen5311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3708"/><hi type="bold">34. Merib-baal--</hi>that is, Mephibosheth. <div eID="gen5311" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f1b322ccd733bd38b2d9e8a37d26979e19bbd81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3709"/><div sID="gen5312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3709"/><hi type="bold">36. Jehoadah--</hi>or, Jara (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.42">1Ch 9:42</reference>). <div eID="gen5312" type="x-p"/>
entries.6edee0c5d0ab38f3a01337980e4e8b8f15e7dd8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3710"/><div sID="gen5313" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3710"/><hi type="bold">40. mighty men of valour, archers--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Judg.20.16">Jud 20:16</reference>). Great strength as well as skill was requisite in ancient archery, as the bow, which was of steel, was bent by treading with the feet, and pulling the string with both hands. <chapter eID="1Chr.8"/>

entries.0c580650fe9096d206505f9d345b8accd6f49991: <div eID="gen13525" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13526" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13527" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13527" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13526" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13528" type="x-p"/> The genealogy of Benjamin down to Saul, vv. 1-32. The children and descendants of Saul, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33-1Chr.8.40">1Chr 8:33-40</reference>. <div eID="gen13528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13529" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13530" type="x-p"/> Now Benjamin begat, etc. - See what has been said on the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.6">1Chr 7:6</reference> (note).
entries.6e05ba450ed342feff6203cec5b19116c6134b3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen13530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13531" type="x-p"/> He begat of Hodesh his wife - In the preceding verse it is said that Hushim and Baara were his wives; and here it is said he begat of Hodesh his wife, etc. And then his children by Hushim are mentioned, but not a word of Baara! It is likely therefore that Hodesh was another name for Baara, and this is asserted by the Targum: And he begot of Baara, that is Chodesh, his wife; so called because he espoused her anew. It is supposed that he had put her away before, and now remarried her.
entries.ea2547154c1c37b2f6b27158bb9442dd9ddf8d41: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen13531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13532" type="x-p"/> Who built Ono, and Lod - The Targum adds, "Which the children of Israel ravaged and burnt with fire, when they made war on the tribe of Benjamin in Gibeah."
entries.37914cff0893dafc6c66d675e4bf38b3465d2086: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen13532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13533" type="x-p"/> These were heads of the fathers - On the following verses Dr. Kennicott has labored hard to restore the true reading. See his detailed comparison of these and their parallel passages in his Hebrew Bible, vol. ii., p. 667.
entries.fc46898588a24f22ad04098f613632eb94ea9158: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen13533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13534" type="x-p"/> And at Gibeon - This passage to the end of the 38th verse is found with a little variety in the names, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35-1Chr.9.44">1Chr 9:35-44</reference>. <div eID="gen13534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13535" type="x-p"/> The rabbins say that Ezra, having found two books that had these passages with a variety in the names, as they agreed in general, he thought best to insert them both, not being able to discern which was the best. <div eID="gen13535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13536" type="x-p"/> His general plan was to collate all the copies he had, and to follow the greater number when he found them to agree; those which disagreed from the majority were thrown aside as spurious; and yet, in many cases, probably the rejected copies contained the true text. <div eID="gen13536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13537" type="x-p"/> If Ezra proceeded as R. Sol. Jarchi says, he had a very imperfect notion of the rules of true criticism; and it is no wonder that he has left so many faults in his text.
entries.2c0bc6e2cc728b37e3c47a236f4ca06a1a365a69: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen13537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13538" type="x-p"/> Merib-baal - The same as Mephibosheth, for, as the Israelites detested Baal, which signifies lord, they changed it into bosheth, which signifies shame or reproach.
entries.dfa3f884cf8d4444777e73bad22fd9b0eae47f79: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen13538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13539" type="x-p"/> The sons of Ulam were mighty men of valor - The Targum speaks honourably of them: "The sons of Ulam were mighty and strong men, subduing by wisdom their evil concupiscence, as men bend a bow; therefore they had many sons and grandsons." Of the six sons of Azel, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.38">1Chr 8:38</reference>, R. S. Jarchi says that their allegorical expositions were sufficient to load thirteen thousand camels! No doubt these were reputed to be deeply learned men. There was a time when the allegorizers and metaphor-men ranked very high among theologians, even in our own enlightened and critical country. At present they are almost totally out of fashion. May they never recover their footing! But what a shameful hyperbole is that of Jarchi! The writings of six men a load for thirteen thousand camels!  <chapter eID="1Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen13539" type="x-p"/>

entries.e79d2074986b0e728e0a4c5486fee26809b4bd30: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.1-1Chr.8.2">1Ch 8:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">The sons of Benjamin and Bela.</hi> - The manner in which the five sons begotten by Benjamin are enumerated is remarkable, “Bela his first-born, Ashbel the second,” etc., since, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.46.21">Gen 46:21</reference>, after the first-born Bela, Becher follows as the second son, and Ashbel is the third; while Aharah, Nohah, and Rapha are not met with there, quite other names occupying their place. In אחרח we can easily recognise the אחירם of Num 26:38, whence the enumeration in 1Ch 8:1. harmonizes with the order in Num 26:38. It is therefore clear, that in our genealogy only those sons are mentioned who founded the families of Benjamin. The names נוחה and רפא are nowhere else met with among the sons of Benjamin; but we may conclude, partly from the agreement of the first three names with the heads of the families of Benjamin enumerated in Num 26:38, and partly from the agreement as to the number, which is five in both passages, that נוחה and רפא are intended to correspond to the שׁפוּפם and חוּפם of Num 26:39. The only question which then remains is, whether the variation in the names arises from these two sons of Benjamin having had different names, or from the families which issued from Shephupham and Hupham having afterwards perhaps received new names from famous chiefs, instead of the original designations, so that Nohah and Rapha would be later descendants of Shephupham and Hupham. Even this second supposition seems possible, since הוליד in such genealogical registers may denote mediate procreation. If, e.g., Nohah were a grandson or great-grandson of Shephupham the son of Benjamin, he might well be introduced in the genealogical lists of the families as begotten by Benjamin.
entries.405c409522a285475f3f495e4c7f1999fd762bbc: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.3-1Chr.8.5">1Ch 8:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen5657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5658" type="x-p"/> The sons of Bela. Of the six names borne by these sons, גּרא is twice met with; נעמן is found in <reference osisRef="Gen.46.21">Gen 46:21</reference> as the son, and in Num 26:40 as grandson of Benjamin; שׁפוּפן is another form of שׁפוּפם, Num 26:39; and חוּרם may be a transcriber’s error for chuwpaam, Num 26:39, just as אדּר probably stands for ארדּ, Gen 46:21. The occurrence of the name Gera would be incomprehensible only if בּנים denoted sons in the narrower sense of the word; but if בּנים fi tub are sons in the wider sense, i.e., descendants who founded fathers'-houses (groups of related households), two cousins might have the same name. In that case, Addar, Shephuphan, and Huram also may be different persons from Ard, Shephupham, and Hupham. Abihud and Abishua are met with as descendants of Benjamin only here, and 'achowach may be connected with אחיּה, 1Ch 8:7.
entries.2b23903c74c0201b6c787039c1e35917cce1c0b0: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.6-1Chr.8.7">1Ch 8:6-7</reference> <hi type="italic">Sons of Ehud.</hi> - The descent of Ehud from the sons, grandsons, and descendants of Benjamin, enumerated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.1-1Chr.8.5">1Ch 8:1-5</reference>, is not given. The names of Ehud’s sons follow only at the end of the <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.7">1Ch 8:7</reference>, “And he begat Uzza and Ahihud,” while the intermediate clauses contain historical remarks. These sons were “heads of fathers'-houses of the inhabitants of Geba,” i.e., Geba of Benjamin (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.16">1Sa 13:16</reference>), the Levite city, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.45">1Ch 6:45</reference>, which still remains as the half-ruinous village Jeba, about three leagues to the north of Jerusalem; see on Jos 18:24. “And they led them captive to Manahath, viz., Naaman and Ahiah and Gera, this man led them captive.” The subject to ויּגלוּם are the men mentioned in the following verse, while the הוּא which follows shows that, of the three above mentioned, the last, Gera, was the author of their captivity. The place Manahath is not known, but is conjectured to be connected with Hazi-Hammanahti and Hazi-Hammenuhoth, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.54">1Ch 2:54</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.52">1Ch 2:52</reference>; but we cannot ascertain with certainty whether the name denotes a city or a district, and the situation of it has not yet been discovered. Of the hostile collision of these Benjamite families also, no more detailed accounts have come down to us.
entries.e9d32773d893ddbb991bf1daf75656a6abdea5e0: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.8-1Chr.8.12">1Ch 8:8-12</reference> <hi type="italic">The descendants of Shaharaim.</hi> - The descent of Shaharaim from the sons and grandsons named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.1-1Chr.8.3">1Ch 8:1-3</reference> is obscure, and the conjecture which connects him with Ahishahar of <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.10">1Ch 7:10</reference> is unsupported. He was the father of a considerable number of heads of fathers'-houses, whom his two or three wives bore to him. According to <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.8">1Ch 8:8</reference>, he begat “in the country of Moab after he had sent them, Hushim and Baara his wives, away; (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.9">1Ch 8:9</reference>) there begat he with Hodesh his wife, Jobab,” etc. When and how Shaharaim, a Benjamite, came into the country of Moab, is not known; all that can be gathered from our verse is that he must have lived there for a considerable time. שׁלחו is <hi type="italic">infin. Pi.</hi>, the “<hi type="italic">i</hi>” being retained, and the Daghesh forte omitted with Sheva (cf. as to this formation, Ew. §238, <hi type="italic">d</hi>.). אתם, accus. of the pronoun, which, as it precedes its noun, is in <hi type="italic">gen. masc.</hi>, although the names of women follow (cf. for this use of the pronoun, Ew. §309, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.). חוּשׁים and בּערה are women, as we learn from the following נשׁיו. By this parenthesis, the beginning of the main sentence has been lost sight of, and the הוליד is taken up again in ויּולד. As to הוליד with מן, cf. the remark on 1Ch 2:8. חדשׁ is the third wife, which he took instead of those he had sent away. The seven names in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.9">1Ch 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.10">1Ch 8:10</reference> are grouped together as sons or descendants of the last-named wife, by the concluding remark, “These his sons are heads of fathers'-houses.” Then, further, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.11">1Ch 8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.12">1Ch 8:12</reference>, the sons and grandsons of the first (divorced) wives, one of whom built the cities Ono and Lydda, are enumerated; but we have no means of determining whether the בּנה הוּא refers to Shemer, the last mentioned, or to Elpaal the father of the three sons, Eber, and Misham, and Shemer. It would, however, naturally suggest itself, that the words referred to the first. לד (Lod) is without doubt the city Lydda, where Peter healed the paralytic (Act 9:32.). It belonged in the Syrian age to Samaria, but it was added to Judea by the King Demetrius Soter, and given to Jonathan for a possession (1 Macc. 11:34, cf. with 10:30, 38). In the Jewish was it was destroyed by the Roman general Cestius (Joseph. <hi type="italic">de Bell. Jud.</hi> ii. 19. 1), but was rebuilt at a later time, and became the site of a toparchy of Judea. In still later times it was called Diospolis, but is now a considerable Mohammedan village, lying between Jafa and Jerusalem to the north of Ramleh, which bears the old name Ludd, by the Arabs pronounced also Lidd. See v. Raumer, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> S. 10; Robins. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> <hi type="italic">sub voce;</hi> and Tobler, <hi type="italic">Dritte Wanderung</hi>, S. 69f. Ono is mentioned elsewhere only in Ezr 2:33; <reference osisRef="Neh.7.37">Neh 7:37</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.11.35">Neh 11:35</reference>, along with Lod, and must have been a place in the neighbourhood of Lydda.
entries.1ef0a4e807ee8070f24f8c93d43b7f6c7c0a171a: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13-1Chr.8.14">1Ch 8:13-14</reference> <hi type="italic">Heads of fathers'-houses of the tribe of Benjamin</hi>, who dwelt partly in Aijalon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13">1Ch 8:13</reference>) and partly in Jerusalem. - Their connection with the heads of fathers'-houses already mentioned is not clear. The names ושׁמע בּריעה might be taken fore a fuller enumeration of the sons of Elpaal (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.12">1Ch 8:12</reference>), were it not that the names enumerated from <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.14">1Ch 8:14</reference> or 15 onwards, are at the end of <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.16">1Ch 8:16</reference> said to be those of sons of Beriah; whence we must conclude that with וּבריעה, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13">1Ch 8:13</reference>, a new list of heads of Benjamite fathers'-houses begins. This view is supported by the fact that the names from <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.14">1Ch 8:14</reference> or <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.15">1Ch 8:15</reference> to <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.27">1Ch 8:27</reference> are divided into five groups of families: the sons of Beriah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.16">1Ch 8:16</reference>), of Elpaal (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.18">1Ch 8:18</reference>), of Shimhi (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.21">1Ch 8:21</reference>), of Shashak (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.25">1Ch 8:25</reference>), and of Jeroham (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.27">1Ch 8:27</reference>). But as two of these, Beriah and Shashak, occur in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13">1Ch 8:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.14">1Ch 8:14</reference>, and שׁמעי is probably another form of שׁמע, Bertheau conjectures that the last two names, Shashak and Jeroham, are represented by אחיו and ירמות dna א (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.14">1Ch 8:14</reference>). ירחם and ירמות may be explained by the supposition of a transcriber’s error, or by one person having two names; but the word אחיו is rendered by the lxx by ὁ ἀδελφὸς αὐτοῦ (= אהיו); and the view that אחיו is a <hi type="italic">nom. prop.</hi> is opposed, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.31">1Ch 8:31</reference>, by the fact that the ו cop. is not found before the following שׁשׁק, for here, throughout, the names are all connected with each other by the w cop. Bertheau therefore conjectures that the text originally ran thus, ושׁשׁק אהיו ואלפּעל, and that the name Elpaal was dropped out; and that in consequence of that, אחיו had been punctuated as a <hi type="italic">nom. prop.</hi> These conjectures seem satisfactory, especially as it may be adduced in their favour that אהיו has been added to the name Elpaal to connect the names in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.15">1Ch 8:15</reference> with the enumeration (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13">1Ch 8:13</reference>) interrupted by the parenthetical remarks. No certainty, however, can be attained in a matter so obscure. If a new series of groups of families begins with <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.13">1Ch 8:13</reference>, we should expect an introductory formula, as in 1Ch 8:6. Beriah and Shema are called heads of the fathers'-houses of the inhabitants of Aijalon, i.e., heads of the groups of related households inhabiting Aijalon, the present Jalo to the west of Gibeon (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.19.42">Jos 19:42</reference>). It is quite consistent with this that their sons or descendants dwelt in Jerusalem. Next a heroic deed of theirs is related, viz., that they (in some war or other) turned to flight the inhabitants of Gath (without doubt Philistines). This remark reminds us of the statement in <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.21">1Ch 7:21</reference>, that sons of Ephraim were slain by those born in Gath, because they had gone down to drive away the herds of the inhabitants. But Bertheau draws an erroneous conclusion from this fact, when he says that because in both passages the name Beriah occurs, both refer to the same event, and thereafter attempts by various hypotheses to make the Benjamites mentioned in our verse into Ephraimites. For the name Beriah is not at all so rare as to allow of our inferring from that alone that the various persons so called are identical, for Jacob’s son Asher also named one of his sons Beriah; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.30">1Ch 7:30</reference> with Gen 46:17. The notion that the Benjamites Beriah and Shema defeated those inhabitants of Gath who had slain the sons of Ephraim (<reference osisRef="1Chr.7.21">1Ch 7:21</reference>) is quite unsupported, as the Philistines lived at war and in feud with the Israelites for hundreds of years.
entries.b36a4dfe0523b6db7fa13515d7da596317b26f76: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.15-1Chr.8.16">1Ch 8:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen5658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5659" type="x-p"/> Several of the names of these six sons of Beriah who are mentioned in our verse occur elsewhere, but nowhere else are they met with as sons of Beriah.
entries.3f96bf774662008913aec653ab242b367d99f796: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.17-1Chr.8.28">1Ch 8:17-28</reference> <div eID="gen5659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5660" type="x-p"/> Bertheau would identify three of the sons of Elpaal - Meshullam, Heber, and Ishmerai - with Misham, Eber, and Shemer, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.12">1Ch 8:12</reference>, but without any sufficient reason; for it is questionable if even the Elpaal whose sons are named in our verses be the same person as the Elpaal mentioned in 1Ch 8:12. Of these descendants of Elpaal, also, nothing further is known, and the same may be said of the nine sons of Shimhi, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.19-1Chr.8.21">1Ch 8:19-21</reference>; of the eleven sons of Shashak, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.22-1Chr.8.25">1Ch 8:22-25</reference>; and of the six sons of Jeroham, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.26">1Ch 8:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.27">1Ch 8:27</reference>, although some of these names are met with elsewhere singly. The concluding remark, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.28">1Ch 8:28</reference>, “These are heads of fathers'-houses,” refers, without doubt, to all the names from <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.15">1Ch 8:15</reference> or <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.14">1Ch 8:14</reference> to 1Ch 8:27. “According to their generations - heads” is in apposition to the preceding, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.24">1Ch 9:24</reference>, but the meaning of the apposition is doubtful. The word ראשׁים can hardly be repeated merely for emphasis, as the old commentators understood it, in harmony with the Vulgate <hi type="italic">principes inquam</hi>, for why should this word be so emphasized? Bertheau thinks that “according to their births - heads” is to be taken to mean that those who are enumerated by name are not the heads living at the time of the preparation of this register, but the individual families, with the name of their progenitor after whom they were named in the genealogical lists. But how this meaning can be found in the words in question, I at least cannot understand. Can the individual families be called אבות ראשׁי, “heads of fathers'-houses”? The families are the fathers'-houses themselves, i.e., they are made up of the groups of related households comprehended under the name fathers'-houses. These groups of related households have, it is true, each of them either head, but cannot possibly be themselves called heads. The meaning seems rather to be that the persons named in the family registers, or registers of births, are introduced as heads (of fathers'-houses); and the reason why this is remarked would seem to be, to prevent those who are enumerated as the sons of this or that man from being regarded simply as members of fathers'-houses. The further remark, “these dwelt in Jerusalem,” is manifestly not to be taken to mean that the heads alone dwelt there, while the households that were subordinated to them lived elsewhere; for it signifies that they dwelt in Jerusalem with the households which composed their respective fathers'-houses. That the households dwelt there also is not stated, merely because the register contains only the names of the heads.
entries.085888e8db7bbfed6e6fc8131af55b2ecf339cb5: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.29">1Ch 8:29</reference> <hi type="italic"></hi> - <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.29-1Chr.8.38">1Ch 8:29-38</reference> recur in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35-1Chr.9.44">1Ch 9:35-44</reference> (see on that passage).  <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.29-1Chr.8.32">1Ch 8:29-32</reference> <div eID="gen5660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5661" type="x-p"/> The ancestors of Saul. They dwelt mainly in Gibeon, but a branch of them were settled in Jerusalem, 1Ch 8:32.f. In Gibeon, now El Jib, two hours north-west from Jerusalem (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.9.3">Jos 9:3</reference>), dwelt the father of Gibeon, with his wife and his sons. The plural ישׁבוּ is used because there dwelt there, besides the father of Gibeon, also his wife and his sons. The father, i.e., the lord and possessor of Gibeon, was called, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.35">1Ch 9:35</reference>, Jehiel (יעיאל, Keth. יעואל), and his wife Maachah, a not uncommon female name (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.48">1Ch 2:48</reference>). The descent of Jehiel from Benjamin is not given. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.30">1Ch 8:30</reference> eight names are given as those of his sons, while in 1Ch 9:36. ten are mentioned, the latter statement being correct; for a comparison of the two passages shows that in our verse two names have been dropped out, - Ner between Baal and Nadab, and Mikloth at the end, which must have originally stood in our register also, - for in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.32">1Ch 8:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33">1Ch 8:33</reference> their descendants are mentioned. זכר is called in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.37">1Ch 9:37</reference> זכריה. These names are evidently those of actual sons of Jehiel who were progenitors of fathers'-houses (groups of related households), but in the case of only two is the race descended from these further noticed. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.32">1Ch 8:32</reference> we have that of the youngest Mikloth, who begat Shimeah, called in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.38">1Ch 9:38</reference> Shimeam. These also (viz., Shimeah and his family) dwelt in Jerusalem אחיהם נגד, “before their brethren,” i.e., over against them, and אחיהם עם, “with their brethren.” The brethren are the other Benjamites in the first clause, those dwelling outside of Jerusalem and inhabiting the neighbouring country as far as Gibeon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.30">1Ch 8:30</reference>); in the second, those dwelling in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.28">1Ch 8:28</reference>). From this it is clear that of the descendants of Abi-Gibeon only that branch which was descended from Mikloth went to Jerusalem.
entries.a379531c329bd3226b3c5b3a860c2499b6d93204: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33">1Ch 8:33</reference> <div eID="gen5661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5662" type="x-p"/> The family of Ner. Ner begat Kish, and Kish Saul. According to <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.51">1Sa 14:51</reference>, Kish was a son of Abiel. this statement, on account of which Bertheau proposes to make alterations in the text, may be reconciled with that in our verses, by the simple supposition that in our verse intermediate names mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference>, and probably others besides, are passed over, and Ner the son of Abi-Gibeon is named only because he was the progenitor of the line by which Saul was descended from him. Saul (שׁאוּל) is King Saul. Only three of his four sons, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49">1Sa 14:49</reference>, are mentioned-those, namely, who fell with him in the battle against the Philistines, 1Sa 31:2. The second is called, in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49">1Sa 14:49</reference>, Ishui, but in <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.2">1Sa 31:2</reference> Abinadab, as in our register, whence we gather that Ishui is another name for Abinadab. The fourth, Eshbaal, is the same who is called in <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.8">2Sa 2:8</reference>, and elsewhere, Ishbosheth, who was set up as king in opposition to David by Abner (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.8">2Sa 2:8</reference>).
entries.b218b26070e6339d0f7d63eece610b68fe0f24bb: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.34-1Chr.8.39">1Ch 8:34-39</reference> <div eID="gen5662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5663" type="x-p"/> Jonathan’s sons and grandsons. His son is called here and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.40">1Ch 9:40</reference> Meribbaal, while in <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.6">2Sa 9:6</reference>; 2Sa 16:1., <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.25">2Sa 19:25</reference>, he is called Mephibosheth, because the name “striver with Baal” has been changed into מפיבשׁת, <hi type="italic">exterminans idolum</hi>. This Meribbaal, who was lame in his feet (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference>), had a son Micha (מיכה, in <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.12">2Sa 9:12</reference> written מיכא), of whom came a numerous race. He had four sons (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.35">1Ch 8:35</reference>), and the family of the last-named of these (Ahaz) is traced down, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.36-1Chr.8.40">1Ch 8:36-40</reference>, through ten generations to the great-grandson of Eshek. First it is traced from Ahaz to Alemeth (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.36">1Ch 8:36</reference>); then through Zimri, brother of this latter, to Binea, by הוליד; then further by בּנו (hisson) to Azel, of whom in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.38">1Ch 8:38</reference> six sons are enumerated; and finally, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.39">1Ch 8:39</reference>, the sons of his brother Eshek are named, and the sons and grandsons of the first-born of this latter are then enumerated. The last two verses are wanting after 1Ch 9:44. The names in the two registers correspond, except at one point, where we cannot get rid of the discrepancy that for יחועדּה (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.36">1Ch 8:36</reference>) there stands in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.42">1Ch 9:42</reference> יערה both times, probably through an error of transcription, by which out of the shortened form יעדּה there arose יערה, ד and ר being interchanged. Besides this, instead of the תּארע of <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.35">1Ch 8:35</reference>, we have in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.41">1Ch 9:41</reference>, according to the harder pronunciation of the gutturals, תּחרע; and for רפה, <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.37">1Ch 8:37</reference>, we have in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.41">1Ch 9:41</reference> the longer original form רפיה. Now since Ahaz, whose posterity is traced down to the tenth generation, was descended from Jonathan in the third generation, and his grandfather Mephibosheth was a boy of five years of age at the death of Saul and Jonathan (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.4">2Sa 4:4</reference>), the grandsons of Ulam, mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.40">1Ch 8:40</reference>, will be the thirteenth generation of Jonathan’s descendants. Now Jonathan fell along with Saul in the year 1055 b.c., and consequently this thirteenth generation of Jonathan’s descendants lived probably about 700 b.c., i.e., about 100 years before the Babylonian exile; for, according to the analogy of the royal race of David, we cannot reckon more than twenty-five years on an average for each generation.<note placement="foot">Bertheau holds a contrary opinion to that given in the text, and thinks that by the numerous sons and grandsons of Ulam the son of Eshek we are brought down to post-exilic times, seeing that if Saul lived about 1080 b.c., and thirty years are reckoned to each one of the thirteen generations (Eshek being a descendant of Saul in the thirteenth generation), Azel and Eshek must have lived about 690 b.c. But this estimate is too high, for we cannot reckon sixty years to Saul and Jonathan from 1080 onwards, since Jonathan fell along with Saul in 1055, and his son Meribbaal was then hardly five years old, and must consequently have been born in 1060. For the following generations, moreover, not more than twenty-five years on an average should be reckoned. That being the case, the children’s children of Ulam’s sons, who were the twelfth generation of Micha’s descendants, may have lived from 760 b.c. onwards, and during this period, from 760 to 700, may have increased to the troop of blooming grandchildren of Ulam mentioned in 1Ch 8:40. But even supposing that thirty years should be reckoned for each generation, the last-named generation of 150 grandsons and great-grandsons of Ulam would have lived in the period from 660 to 600, i.e., before the exile, or at least before the first great deportation of the people with Jehoiakim in the year 599 b.c.</note>
entries.58989d34b8e2d09ede2839e499843e8d9c2a8f0a: <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.40">1Ch 8:40</reference> <div eID="gen5663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5664" type="x-p"/> The sons of Ulam are called valiant heroes and archers, and must have shown the same capability for war by which the tribe of Benjamin had been distinguished at an earlier time; cf. Jdg 20:16, and for קשׁת דּרכי, cf. 1Ch 5:16. The subscription כּל־אלּה מ refers back to the superscription in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.1">1Ch 8:1</reference>, and binds all the names in our chapter together. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1-1Chr.9.3">1Ch 9:1-3</reference> form the transition from the genealogies to the enumeration of the former inhabitants of Jerusalem in vv. 4-34.  <chapter eID="1Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen5664" type="x-p"/>
